hypothesis: Ordering internal alpha-beta children by the unchanged static Baseline A evaluator reduces expanded search nodes and wall-clock time without changing any chosen action.
ordering_policy: At maximizing nodes search the highest one-ply static evaluation first; at minimizing nodes search the lowest first. Root action order and lexicographic tie-breaking remain unchanged.
interpretation: Action equivalence held at every tested frozen position for depths 2, 3, and 4.
At depth 2 there is no internal alpha-beta pruning opportunity below the root, so ordering changed no node counts and added about 39 percent latency overhead.

At depth 3 static ordering reduced expanded nodes by 36.2 percent across the suite and never increased node count at any position, but the extra one-ply evaluations made total wall-clock time about 83.3 percent slower than baseline.

At depth 4 static ordering reduced expanded nodes by 46.6 percent across the suite, with node reduction at all 16 positions, but total wall-clock time was still about 27.2 percent slower than baseline.
The pruning hypothesis is strongly supported, but using the full static evaluator as the ordering heuristic is too expensive to count as a runtime improvement by itself.

This result justifies a cheaper ordering heuristic experiment before promoting move ordering into the product engine. The important signal is that Crownline's search tree is highly order-sensitive at depths 3 and 4.
